title: In Praise of Boredom
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Anthony B. Bradley synthesizes research on boredom, mind-wandering, and creativity to make the case that boredom is not an educational problem to be eliminated but a developmental resource to be protected. The piece reviews studies showing that boredom consistently activates the default mode network (DMN) -- the brain's 'mind-wandering' circuitry -- which is associated with creative problem-solving, autobiographical memory consolidation, empathy development, and planning for the future. Children who never experience boredom because their attention is continuously captured by screens and structured activities are not being enriched; they are being deprived of the unstructured mental time that these foundational cognitive processes require. Bradley traces the disappearance of boredom from childhood in parallel with the rise of smartphone use and argues that the two are causally connected. The piece closes with specific practices for protecting children's boredom: unstructured outdoor time, phone-free evenings, and explicit resistance to the cultural pressure to fill every moment with stimulation.
points: * Boredom activates the default mode network (DMN), which is responsible for creative problem-solving, autobiographical memory consolidation, empathy development, and future planning -- cognitive processes that require unstructured mental time to function. * Children who never experience boredom because attention is continuously captured by screens and structured activities are deprived of the unstructured mental time that these foundational developmental processes require. * The disappearance of boredom from childhood is causally connected to smartphone use: the phone's capacity to fill every second of idle time is also the capacity to prevent every second of DMN activation. * Mind-wandering is not unfocused attention; it is a different kind of focused attention -- turned inward, prospective, integrative -- that does work that directed attention cannot do. * Bradley's practical recommendations include protecting unstructured outdoor time, enforcing phone-free evenings, and explicitly resisting the cultural pressure to fill every moment with stimulation or organized activity.
quotes: Boredom is not a problem to be solved. It is a condition to be protected. When your child says 'I'm bored,' they are telling you their default mode network is coming online. They are telling you that the interesting cognitive work is about to start -- the daydreaming, the integrating, the imagining. The correct response is not to hand them a screen.

The default mode network is not idle brain activity. It is a specific set of neural processes that are suppressed by directed attention and activated by its absence. Creative insights, empathy, autobiographical memory consolidation, future planning -- these are DMN functions. They require the mental space that boredom creates.

We have conducted an uncontrolled experiment on childhood. We have equipped children with devices that can fill every moment of idle time. We have, in doing so, eliminated the idle time that their brains need for foundational developmental processes. The results are coming in, and they are not good.

Mind-wandering is not the same as distraction. Distraction is the failure to maintain intended focus. Mind-wandering is intentional engagement with internal rather than external stimuli. The mind that wanders productively is doing something the focused mind cannot do. It needs the space to do it.

The most countercultural thing you can do for your child right now is to refuse to fill the silence. Let them be bored. Sit with their complaint that there is nothing to do. Do not solve the problem. The discomfort of boredom is the price of admission to the cognitive work that only boredom enables.
